column3: It nearly repeats the focus's dialogue between weak followers and arrogant leaders, then states that neither can escape punishment.
The Day when truthfulness benefits its people gives only a broad judgment-day contrast to the speakers in the Fire.
Its command to follow the recitation shares the language of following but not the focus's burdened leader-follower relation.
The arrogant explicitly deny blocking the weak from guidance, directly extending the dispute and responsibility at issue in the focus.
The disappearance of alleged partners gives nearby surah context for the failure of false attachments at judgment.
Following charity with harm concerns ethical giving, not whether leaders can relieve followers in the Fire.
Those in the Fire ask its keepers for even a day's relief, directly paralleling the focus's request that others bear some punishment.
Divine mercy is a general exception to judgment but does not clarify the speakers' appeal to their leaders.
Its statement that nothing protects from flame supports the focus's failed hope for relief from the Fire.
Weak followers tell arrogant leaders that they would have believed but for them, directly staging the same blame relation before judgment.
The believer contrasts calling people to God with being called to the Fire, supplying an immediate alternative to the path behind the focus.
Self-sufficiency contrasts with the weakness exposed in the focus, but it does not address responsibility or punishment.
The weak blame the arrogant for ordering disbelief, while both conceal regret at punishment, directly clarifying shared but differentiated guilt.
Associating another deity with God does not itself illuminate the followers' request for a share of punishment.
It forbids obeying one who follows desire, providing a practical contrast to the followers' disastrous allegiance.
The arrogant confront weak believers over the messenger, furnishing a living-world counterpart to the focus's hierarchy in the Fire.
The wrongdoers' excuses will not benefit them, reinforcing the futility of the appeal made in the focus.
Miserly self-sufficiency is only an indirect trait contrast to the arrogant and weak in the focus.
The people of the Garden address the people of the Fire after the promise proves true, supplying a related final-judgment dialogue.
The Day when neither schemes nor help avail gives a broad counterpart to the focus's request for aid.
Both the seeker and the sought are weak, a pointed theological reason that invoked powers cannot rescue the followers.
The arrogant threaten worldly expulsion, which only distantly resembles the focus's punishment setting.
The opening statement about revelation does not add to the Fire dialogue or its social accountability.
Divine independence from human disbelief does not clarify whether leaders can bear followers' punishment.
Choosing misguidance and seeking to mislead others supplies a general antecedent to the focus's blame.
The instruction to return greetings does not illuminate the focus.
Those in the Fire ask that whoever brought them there receive doubled punishment, directly extending the allocation of blame among the condemned.
Protective armor in worldly conflict does not clarify relief from the Fire.
The angels pray that the righteous enter the Garden, an immediate-surah contrast to the condemned followers' condition.
No one can pursue a claim against God after punishment, broadly limiting the displaced responsibility sought in the focus.
Calling disbelievers better guided is a general instance of misguiding judgment, not the Fire dispute.
The request for idols gives a remote antecedent to false allegiance but adds little after the direct parallels.
Divine ownership and independence do not clarify the focus's plea.
Each party bears its own deeds, directly countering the followers' hope that leaders can absorb their consequence.
The same-surah rule of proportionate recompense frames why a share of punishment cannot simply be transferred away.
Leaders who drew others after them bear disgrace through the Hereafter, supporting responsibility for misleading followers.
The judgment question about alleged partners supplies a related exposure of misplaced loyalties.
Mindful people remembering God after temptation does not clarify the focus's post-punishment dispute.
Wealth and children cannot avail disbelievers before God and they remain in the Fire, directly supporting the failure of any substitute protection.
Those who led others astray admit that they themselves were astray, directly clarifying leaders' role in the focus's accusation.
Warning of the Day of Meeting gives nearby judgment context but not the particular exchange in the Fire.
Following God's pleasure is contrasted with a destination in Hell, offering a concise contrary path to the focus's allegiance.
When punishment arrives, wrongdoers ask for delay to follow the messengers, closely paralleling belated recognition and a futile request for change.
The question whether false gods can help or help themselves directly challenges the possibility of rescue sought in the focus.
Moses asking to follow a teacher concerns learning, not harmful allegiance or punishment.
The call to submit to the one God is a broad corrective to the disbelief underlying the focus.
The believer's call to salvation versus the call to the Fire is immediate context for the choices whose outcome appears in the focus.
Rejecting clear messengers and turning away supplies an antecedent cause of the final rejection and punishment.
Denial of resurrection, shackles, and lasting Fire supplies a related doctrinal and punitive horizon.
The condemned declare that they have no intercessors, directly reinforcing the focus's failure to find another to relieve them.
Food that cannot satisfy hunger does not clarify moral responsibility or the Fire dialogue.
Satan's claimed allotted share does not illuminate the focus's request for a share of punishment.
The world is temporary and the Hereafter enduring, providing nearby-surah context for the irreversible setting of the focus.
Worldly enjoyment proves unable to avail its recipients at consequence, broadly reinforcing the failure of supposed supports.
Assigning provision to false associates and being questioned about it supplies only a general idolatry-accountability link.
The absence of a devoted friend among the condemned directly parallels the lack of help from the leaders addressed in the focus.
God's reversal of the oppressed into leaders contrasts the focus's powerless followers and their dependence on arrogant rulers.
Leaning toward wrongdoers brings the Fire and leaves no protectors, directly warning against the allegiance displayed in the focus.
Divine signs and remembrance give nearby-surah background but do not add to the Fire exchange.
Wrongdoers may support one another, yet cannot avail before God, closely qualifying the mutual dependence presumed in the focus.
Being diverted from remembrance and prayer is a broad cause of wrongdoing, not a direct leader-follower relation.
The allocation of shares from intercession does not address the condemned leaders' inability to bear punishment.
Being pursued during the Exodus does not clarify the focus's following in the Fire.
Believers ask to be turned away from Hell's punishment, a faithful preemptive contrast to the condemned speakers' late appeal.
Pharaoh claims to guide his people while asking who could protect from God's punishment, directly foreshadowing deceptive leadership and failed protection.
Following later generations concerns succession of destroyed peoples, not the focus's social dependence.
The judgment question about answering messengers supplies an accountability setting behind the focus's condemnation.
Provision and feeding the poor do not clarify the Fire dialogue.
The ethics of charitable spending and divine independence do not add to the focus.
Receiving the record in the right hand gives a general contrast to the condemned group's judgment outcome.
The preceding verse places Pharaoh's people before the Fire and then in severer punishment, directly setting the scene for the focus.
Those rebuked for their gathering and arrogance learn it did not avail them, directly undermining the leaders' presumed capacity to help followers.
The false division of provision between God and partners is not a focused explanation of the Fire dispute.
God's judgment among groups on the Day of Resurrection supplies only broad eschatological context.
Wealth does not avail when its owner falls, a compact general parallel to the focus's question whether anything can avail.
Regret on receiving the record in the left hand gives only a general counterpart to the speakers' punishment.
No close friend or accepted intercessor exists for wrongdoers, directly reinforcing the hopeless appeal within the same surah.
The parable of a ruined garden and weak descendants does not clarify the focus's punishment or blame exchange.
The primordial acknowledgment of God removes the possibility of later ignorance, relevant to the accountability exposed in the focus.
At death, idolaters admit their false gods have vanished and testify against themselves, closely paralleling final self-condemnation after misplaced allegiance.
Wealth and children cannot avail disbelievers, who become fuel for the Fire, directly confirming the inability of worldly supports to protect.
The accusation that the messenger is bewitched does not clarify the leaders' inability to relieve followers.
The decisive coming of God's command and loss of falsifiers gives nearby-surah judgment context but no direct relation.
What people earned did not avail them at punishment, a broad parallel to failed sources of protection.
The compelled destination of disbelievers to the Fire gives a general punishment outcome without the focus's social dispute.
No ally can avail another and none are helped on that Day, directly answering the followers' appeal to their leaders.
Conjecture does not avail against truth, a conceptual but remote parallel to futile reliance.
Submission brings guidance while turning away leaves only delivery of the message, a broad antecedent contrast.
The appearance of self-sufficiency among restrained poor people does not illuminate the focus.
People under punishment ask for it to be removed and profess belief, a related but less final plea for relief.
Repentance declared at death is not accepted and disbelievers face painful punishment, directly clarifying the lateness of the focus's appeal.
The misguided follow poets, supplying a general example of harmful followers being led by others.
A community's threat against messengers does not clarify the focus's Fire dialogue.
Wrongdoers follow desires without knowledge and have no helpers, a broad antecedent and outcome parallel to the focus.
God judging religious disputes on the Day of Resurrection gives only general judgment context.
Repeated rejection of messengers and its ruin supplies a broad historical antecedent to final punishment.
Communities are seized for their deeds after denial, a general accountability background.
Lifeless objects cannot answer a call or follow guidance, only distantly echoing the failure of sought help.
The mention of blissful gardens does not add to the focus's scene in the Fire.
Following a means on a journey does not clarify harmful social following or punishment.
The arrogant answer that all are in the Fire and God has judged between servants, directly resolving the focus's request for them to bear a share.
The followed leaders disown their followers when punishment is seen and all ties are cut, directly clarifying the collapse of protective allegiance.
Followers wish for another return so they can disown those they followed, directly extending the focus's remorseful dependency.
Each community entering the Fire curses its sister until the later group asks for doubled punishment for those who led them astray.
The earlier group tells the later that neither has an advantage and both must taste punishment for what they earned, directly rejecting transferred liability.
Satan disavows power over those who followed his call and tells them to blame themselves, sharply delimiting the leaders' responsibility invoked in the focus.
Those who mislead without knowledge carry their own burdens and some burdens of those they mislead, directly distinguishing shared responsibility.
The condemned confess that misery overcame them and that they were astray, supplying the admission preceding their request to leave the Fire.
The people of the Fire ask to be brought out and promise reform, the closest direct parallel to the focus's hope for relief from punishment.
The command to remain in the Fire supplies the explicit negative outcome of the appeal anticipated in the focus.
Those against whom judgment is due say that they led others astray only as they themselves strayed, directly exposing derivative leadership.
Disbelievers invite believers to follow their way and promise to carry their sins, directly testing the false offer of transferred responsibility.
The misleaders will carry their own burdens and additional burdens for those they misled, directly clarifying accountability in harmful following.
As faces are turned in the Fire, the condemned say they obeyed God and the Messenger, directly framing the loss caused by contrary obedience.
The condemned say they obeyed their leaders and great ones, who led them astray, an especially close direct parallel to the focus's followers.
They ask that their leaders receive double punishment and a great curse, directly extending the focus's demand for leaders to bear consequences.
No bearer bears another's burden, directly constraining the focus's request that leaders take a portion of their followers' punishment.
The condemned turn to one another questioning, directly supplying the reciprocal dispute that unfolds in the focus.
Followers tell their leaders that they used to come to them from the right, directly describing the influence later contested in the focus.
The leaders answer that the followers were not believers, directly presenting their denial of coercive responsibility.
The leaders say they had no authority over the followers, directly qualifying the followers' claim against them.
The word of punishment is realized over both groups, directly confirming their shared consequence.
The condemned curse those who prepared the Fire for them and ask for doubled punishment, directly paralleling conflict over responsibility in the Fire.
The people who disbelieved ask to see the jinn and humans who led them astray so they may place them beneath their feet, directly extending blame toward misleaders.
The companion denies having caused the condemned person's transgression and calls him far astray, directly echoing the leaders' defense in a judgment dispute.
God forbids disputing before Him after the warning was sent, directly limiting the value of the blame exchange found in the focus.
God's word is not changed and He is not unjust to servants, directly grounding the finality and justice of the shared punishment.
The intercession of intercessors does not benefit the condemned, directly reinforcing the failure to obtain relief from another party.
